title: Wood Is Built Mostly From Air and Water

scenes.tts: A tulip poplar seed weighs, on average, less than a tenth of a gram. One tulip poplar in a Virginia forest grew so big that scientists estimated about ten thousand kilograms of dry wood. That is an estimate from a model, not a weighing. So where did all that wood come from?

scenes.tts: A deer cannot make its own food. It has to eat. A plant does not eat, yet it grows. A producer is a living thing that makes its own food. Green plants, algae and phytoplankton are producers. Phytoplankton are tiny producers that drift in water.
scenes.visual: A deer with an eat arrow; a plant with no eat arrow; the word producer appears with the three producer labels.
scenes.narration: A deer cannot make its own food. It has to eat. A plant does not eat, yet it grows. A producer is a living thing that makes its own food. Green plants, algae and phytoplankton are producers. Phytoplankton are tiny producers that drift in water.

scenes.tts: Producers make food by photosynthesis. Photosynthesis uses the energy of sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen. The energy in sunlight is radiant energy. It is energy that travels as light. In this summary the sugar is glucose, a small sugar molecule that stores energy.
scenes.visual: The word equation builds from chips: carbon dioxide + water + radiant energy turns into sugar (glucose) + oxygen; light-ray arrows travel in.
scenes.narration: Producers make food by photosynthesis. Photosynthesis uses the energy of sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen. The energy in sunlight is radiant energy. scenes.tts: In plants and algae, photosynthesis happens inside a chloroplast. A chloroplast is a green part of a cell, mostly in leaves. It holds chlorophyll, a green pigment that captures radiant energy. Roots take in water from the soil. Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air, through tiny openings. Carbon dioxide is only a tiny part of air, about zero point zero four percent.

scenes.tts: Once a plant has sugar, it can do three things with it. It can use it now. It can store it as starch. Or it can rearrange it into other compounds, such as the wood of its trunk and the parts of new leaves. Light, carbon dioxide and temperature change how fast photosynthesis goes.
scenes.visual: A sugar chip splits into three arrows: use it now, store it as starch (roots, seeds, leaves), rearrange it into wood and new leaves; three condition chips (light, carbon dioxide, temperature) appear last.
scenes.narration: Once a plant has sugar, it can do three things with it. It can use it now. It can store it as starch. Or it can rearrange it into other compounds, such as the wood of its trunk and the parts of new leaves. Light, carbon dioxide and temperature change how fast photosynthesis goes.

scenes.tts: So where did the tulip poplar's wood come from? The tree built it mostly from carbon dioxide from the air, and from water. Leaves used radiant energy to join them into sugar, and the tree rebuilt the sugar into wood. The soil gave water and a few minerals. So the soil did not need to shrink by thousands of kilograms.
